name: Central Grebo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Grebo has a system of four tone levels; tone is not marked in Grebo writing, but in this book, where it is necessary to mark tone, this will be shown by numerals. The method of tone marking is: 1. High tone is marked with 1: kg 1 chief 2. High-mid tone is marked with 2: bi 2 beat 3. Low-mid tone is marked with 3: ya 3 bring 4. Low tone is marked with 4: pu 4 swell. Gliding tones are marked with a combination of two (or, rarely, three) numerals joined by a hyphen: hu 3-2 throw
new_statements.citation: Innes, Gordon. 1966. An Introduction to Grebo. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: the Innes 1966 'Tone' passage is present verbatim in (lines 'Grebo has a system of four tone levels; tone is not marked in Grebo writing, but in this book, where it is necessary to mark tone, this will be shown by numerals. The method of tone marking is : 1. High tone is marked with 1 : kg 1 chief... Gliding tones are marked with a combination of two (or, rarely, three) numerals joined by a hyphen: hu 3-2 throw'), page footer '12'; the PDF text layer (extracted text, p. 3 of 5) carries the same text. 'kg 1' etc. are scanned artefacts of the numeral tone marks. READING: agree, tone-language-no-stress-statement. The excerpt (ch. 1 pp. 11-13, ch. 2 pp. 14-15) says nothing about stress;…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Grebo (Glebo/Seaside dialect) is a four-level register tone language with lexical and grammatical tone (contour tones, verb tone classes, 1st vs 2nd person pronouns distinguished by tone). Neither this nor any other opened source mentions word stress, stress placement, or the absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress not discussed at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is given on citation forms and in phrases (pronoun tone varies by context). Source describes Glebo = Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826, not Central Grebo [grv]; only pp. 11-15 of the phonological chapters are in the open excerpt, so a stress remark on pp. 16-19 cannot be excluded.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog/Ethnologue split Grebo into five ISO languages; Central Grebo [grv] cent2041 (dialects Nyenebo, Dorobo, Borobo, Trembo) has no grammar, phonology or sketch of its own (Glottolog n_desc_refs = 0). Every phonological description of 'Grebo' (Innes 1960/1966/1967/1981, Luckau 1975, Sapir 1931 on Jabo/Gweabo, Wilson 1838, Payne 1860/1864, Auer 1870, Müller 1877, Christaller 1890) is of Glebo/Seaside Grebo of Cape Palmas or of Jabo, which Glottolog codes as Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826. The quoted Innes 1966 statement therefore belongs to sout2826, not cent2041.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 12 (Orthography, 'Tone'): 'Grebo has a system of four tone levels; tone is not marked in Grebo writing...'; tones marked with numerals 1-4, glides 3-2 etc. Ch. 2 Sounds excerpt (pp. 14-15) covers consonants, vowels, root shapes CV/CVV/CVCV only; the rest of the chapter (pp. 16-19) is not in the open excerpt. Describes Glebo (informant J. Y. Dennis) = Southern Grebo [grj] sout2826.

sources.citation: Payne, John. 1860. A Dictionary of the Grebo Language. New York: Edward O. Jenkins. 100 pp. (Google/NYPL scan)
sources.note: Only a pronunciation key (vowel/consonant values, nasals); no accent/stress statement; introduction p. 6 says the diacritics do not capture 'many shades of sound and intonation, only to be apprehended in a thorough acquaintance with the spoken language'. Cape Palmas Grebo = Southern Grebo.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 pages for cent2041 (Central Grebo) and sout2826 (Southern Grebo); WALS languoid grb (Grebo = grj)
sources.note: cent2041 lists no descriptive references (subclassification comments cite Vogler 2017:15-18 and Johnson & Hasselbring 2002); sout2826 alt. name Jabo. WALS Grebo cites Innes 1966, Innes 1967, Sapir 1931, Marchese 1988; no stress feature values shown.
Says tone is 'extremely important' (né 'I' vs nè 'you'); nothing on stress; references Innes 1966/1967 and Payne 1860.

sources.citation: Christaller, J. G. 1889/90. Näheres über die Kru-Sprache. Zeitschrift für afrikanische Sprachen 3: 1-39 (compiled from Auer 1870 Elements of the Gedebo Language and Crocker's Basa grammar)
sources.note: No stress statement. §1 (p. 2): 'Die Accente. Gravis und Akut für tiefen und hohen Ton, müssen die 1. und 2. Person des Pronomens... unterscheiden'; §5 (p. 3): 'Tiefer und hoher Ton wird... mit Gravis und Akut bezeichnet.' Gedebo/Cape Palmas = Southern Grebo; second-hand from Auer.

sources.citation: Müller, Friedrich. 1877. Die Sprachen Basa, Grebo und Kru im westlichen Afrika. Sitzungsberichte der kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Wien, phil.-hist. Classe 86(5): 85-102
sources.note: No word-stress rule. p. 94: 'Der lautliche Unterschied zwischen der ersten und zweiten Person besteht in der stärkeren Betonung der letzteren z. B.: mi ne,ich gehe', dagegen mí ne,du gehst'' — a pronoun tone contrast (cf. Innes 1966:13) described as stronger 'Betonung'; based on Payne's Cape Palmas (Southern) Grebo.
